title: Templates and Control Flow
summary: Interpolation, template expressions and Angular's built-in control flow: @if, @for with track, @switch, @empty and @let, plus the context variables inside loops.
introduction: A template is HTML that Angular reads once and keeps alive: every expression in it is re-evaluated when the signals it depends on change. To show something conditionally or repeat it for each item in a list you use the built-in control flow blocks, which look like TypeScript and compile to efficient DOM updates. This lesson covers interpolation, the rules for expressions, and each block with a working example and its rendered result.
learningObjectives: Write interpolations and know which expressions a template allows
Render content conditionally with @if, @else if, @else and @switch
Repeat elements with @for, choose a correct track expression and handle empty lists

blocks.text: Double curly braces evaluate an expression and insert the result as text: `{{ user().name }}`, `{{ price * quantity }}`, `{{ title | uppercase }}`. Template expressions are a deliberately small subset of TypeScript. You can read properties, call methods and signals, use arithmetic, comparison, the ternary operator, `??` and `?.`, and apply pipes. You cannot assign (`=`), increment (`++`), use `new` or arrow functions, or chain statements with `;`. If an expression needs any of those, compute the value in the class, preferably as a `computed()` signal.
Angular escapes interpolated text, so `{{ 'hi' }}` renders the literal characters `hi` rather than bold text. That is what makes templates safe against script injection.
`@if` renders its block only while the condition is true. When it becomes false, the elements are removed from the DOM entirely, not hidden, and any child components inside are destroyed.

`@for` repeats its block once per item. The `track` expression is mandatory: it tells Angular how to identify each item, so that when the array changes it can move, keep or remove the existing DOM nodes instead of rebuilding the whole list. Use a stable unique value such as an `id`. The `@empty` block renders when the collection has no items.

blocks.text: You can read the variables directly (`{{ $index }}`) or alias them with `let`, as the example does, which is clearer in nested loops.

blocks.title: Common mistake: tracking by index or forgetting track
blocks.text: Leaving `track` out is a compile error: `NG5002: @for loop must have a "track" expression`. Writing `track $index` compiles, but when an item is removed from the middle of the list every following item is re-rendered and any state inside those rows (a focused input, an expanded panel) jumps to the wrong row. Track by an id whenever items can be added, removed or reordered; use `track item` only for lists of primitives that never change order.
When one value selects between several blocks, `@switch` reads better than a chain of `@else if`. Cases are compared with `===` and there is no fall-through, so no `break` is needed.

blocks.text: `@let` declares a variable inside the template. It is useful when an expression is needed several times, or when a value should be computed once per render rather than in three separate interpolations. The variable is available from the line it is declared until the end of the enclosing block.

blocks.text: Before Angular 17, conditionals and loops were written with structural directives: `*ngIf="ready"`, `*ngFor="let task of tasks"` and `[ngSwitch]`, all imported from `@angular/common`. They still work, so you will meet them in older code and answers online, but the block syntax is faster, needs no imports and is type-checked more precisely. Existing projects can convert automatically with `ng generate @angular/core:control-flow`.

questions.question: Which `track` expression is the best choice for a list of users that can be deleted and re-sorted?
questions.explanation: An id identifies each user no matter where it sits in the list, so Angular can keep the right DOM nodes. `$index` changes when the order changes.
options: No track is needed for small lists

questions.question: When an `@if` condition becomes false, Angular hides the elements with `display: none` but keeps them in the DOM.
questions.explanation: The block's elements are removed from the DOM and any components inside are destroyed. Use a class binding if you only want to hide something.
